Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Vignette:
Six years ago, Davin Tran was detained in a windowless holding facility while investigating a cross-border smuggling ring. The captors did not rely on isolated incidents of violence; they engineered an environment of sustained psychological pressure. For weeks, Davin was confined to a lower cell where the muffled cries of children bleeding through the floorboards became a constant, inescapable backdrop. When he was moved to an upper room for interrogations, he was made to endure prolonged physical restraint and forced breathing patterns that left his equilibrium permanently unsteady, so that even normal shifts in his environment now triggered sudden waves of lightheadedness. The guards rarely spoke directly at first. Instead, they read aloud from a ledger, repeating the names of journalists who had previously covered the region, and later the designation of the facility itself, until the phonetics alone carried immediate threat. Davin remembered the cold concrete against his spine, the moment his own voice gave out during coerced statements, and the days when the darkness simply swallowed time, leaving him with no recollection of what transpired. He also knew the interrogation had forced him to sign documents that contradicted everything he had spent his life defending. When Davin returned to his work as a journalist, the newsroom’s rhythm felt like a different country. He began sitting near the glass partition that faced the stairwell, his chair angled so he could track every person entering the open-plan office. The daily chorus of ringing phones and slamming file cabinets made him jump, his shoulders hiking toward his ears before his brain could confirm nothing was coming for him. He watched the colleagues who used to share morning coffee with him, scanning their postures for shifts in aggression, but he never approached the break room. He stopped eating there, skipping breakfast and lunch to avoid the shared tables where he had once traded bylines and stories. Instead, he carried two plain crackers to his desk and chewed slowly until his stomach stopped cramping, a habit that had thickened over months into a quiet routine of restriction. When he tried to sit down and reconstruct the timeline for his editor, his pen would hover over the page. He would press his palms flat against the desk and try to pull the memories forward, but the footage would dissolve into static. Parts of the facility simply vanished. What remained felt detached, like a report written about someone else, impossible to reconcile with the life he had built since. In the quiet hours, he would loop through his editorial decisions of those final weeks, rehearsing alternate routes and delayed assignments, certain that a different choice could have kept him out of that basement. Lately, the detachment had bled into his daily life. Walking through the farmer’s market near his apartment, a sudden cry from a toddler at a produce stall made his breath catch; his vision swam, and the ground felt unsteady until he gripped a wooden crate and forced his pulse to slow. He avoided the quarterly press club dinners, slipping out early when he realized the guest speaker’s first name matched the one used in the ledger, the syllables echoing in his chest long after the room grew quiet. He carried a heavy shame about the signatures he had affixed under duress, convinced that his integrity had been fundamentally compromised. To his colleagues, his face looked pale, his posture rigid, but to Davin, it felt as though his captivity was etched across his skin, visible in the tightness of his jaw and the flinch in his hands. He had come to believe that he was inherently fractured, that the man who had survived the cell could never quite return to the writer who valued courage and honesty. The newsroom’s morning briefings had always been his anchor, but over time he stopped attending, and his editor quietly reassigned him to archival work. His marriage had been built on shared commutes and weekend interviews; when he stopped sharing those routines, the silence between them simply accumulated until the legal papers arrived. Now, sitting in his therapist’s office, Davin finally asked for help not because the symptoms had lessened, but because the quiet had become too loud. He hoped to stop jumping at ordinary sounds, to stop rationing food to keep his fear at bay, and to find a way to look at his colleagues without scanning for threats. Most of all, he feared that if he stopped running from the memories, the gaps would never fill, and he would be left with only the certainty that he had failed himself when it mattered most.
